title: 5. The Thousand Brains Theory
intro: Jeff Hawkins and colleagues at Numenta propose that every cortical column learns complete models of objects, using reference frames to place features at locations, and that columns vote to reach a shared percept.

blocks.text: Close your eyes and run a finger over a coffee mug. Each touch gives you a small patch of sensation — a curved surface, an edge, the handle — and yet after two or three touches you know it is a mug. Grab it with your whole hand and you may recognise it at once. The Thousand Brains Theory explains both observations with one idea: each patch of sensor feeds a cortical column that knows where on the object it is touching, so each column can learn and recognise whole objects as arrangements of features at locations. One column needs several movements to narrow down the possibilities; many columns touching different places at once can share their guesses and agree in a single step.

This builds directly on HTM (section 4). In HTM's temporal memory, distal dendritic segments let a cell predict its next input from the sequence context. In the Thousand Brains Theory the same mechanism predicts the next input from a location context instead: if I am at this location on this object, I expect this feature. Hawkins, Ahmad & Cui (2017) introduced the column model with an allocentric location signal; Lewis et al. (2019) proposed that the location signal comes from grid-cell-like modules in the cortex; Hawkins et al. (2019) and the book A Thousand Brains (Hawkins 2021) set out the full framework. Since 2024 the open-source Thousand Brains Project has been building a sensorimotor learning system, Monty, on these principles.

Status of the claims: grid cells, place cells and path integration in the entorhinal–hippocampal system are experimentally established. That cortical columns contain grid-cell-like location codes, that layer 6 carries the location signal and layer 4 the sensory feature, that displacement cells exist, and that columns vote through layer 2/3 long-range connections, are theoretical proposals that are not yet established. The pages in this section say which is which.
Pages in this section, in learning order

items: Reference Frames — why the theory puts location at the centre: objects stored as features at locations in object-centric reference frames, and why that helps generalisation and compositional structure.

Grid and Displacement Cells — grid cells, path integration, and the proposal that cortical columns use grid-cell-like modules to encode locations on objects, plus hypothetical displacement cells for relations between objects.

Sensorimotor Object Recognition — recognising an object by moving a sensor over it: feature-location pairs, a shrinking set of candidate objects, and how movement drives inference. Interactive: a single column needing several sensations.

Voting Between Columns — how columns that sense different parts of an object reach consensus through lateral connections, and why that allows recognition in one glance. Interactive: multi-column voting with a sensations-versus-columns curve.
Monty and the Thousand Brains Project — the open-source implementation: sensor modules, learning modules, the Cortical Messaging Protocol, and how to experiment with it.

blocks.text: Why this matters for building a column

If you are building a spiking column aimed at a mini brain, the Thousand Brains Theory gives a concrete target for what each column should compute and a reason to build many columns rather than one large network. It also tells you what extra machinery a column needs beyond a sequence memory: a location signal driven by movement (path integration), a way to associate sensed features with locations (dendritic segments in the sensory layer), and lateral connections between columns that represent each column's current set of candidate objects. Each of these has a plausible spiking implementation — continuous attractor networks or oscillatory phase codes for grid-like locations, NMDA-like dendritic subunits for feature-location association, and excitatory lateral connections plus inhibition for voting — which the pages sketch and Section 7's "Step-by-Step Roadmap" stages.

items: Each column learns complete object models, not just fragments that are assembled higher up a hierarchy.
Objects are stored as features at locations in object-centric reference frames; the location signal is updated by movement.
A single column recognises objects by integrating several sensations over movements; many columns can recognise in one step by voting.
The anatomical mapping (L4 features, L6 locations, L2/3 voting) is a hypothesis, not an established fact.
Monty is the reference implementation to read and run before building your own spiking version.
